stories.author: cisc
stories.title: The Most Popular Car Colors in America
stories.groq_label: White leads U.S. car color popularity, with grayscale colors capturing over 80% of the market.
stories.groq_explain:
The article presents findings from an iSeeCars study that examined the colors of more than 22 million used vehicles produced between 1996 and 2025, based on sales from January 2025 through May 2026. The purpose of the study is to identify the most popular car colors in the United States and to track how color preferences have shifted over the past three decades.

White is the leading color in 2025, holding a 25.7 percent market share, followed by black at 23.4 percent and gray at 22.9 percent. Together these three grayscale shades account for roughly 72 percent of all cars. When silver is added, the four grayscale colors—white, black, gray and silver—make up 80.4 percent of the market, a dramatic increase from 47.3 percent in 1996. The rise of grayscale colors has been especially pronounced for gray, which grew from 3.6 percent to 22.9 percent, a gain of more than 500 percent. Black also saw a large increase, while white’s share rose steadily after 2010.

Conversely, bright and non‑grayscale colors have lost ground. Red fell from 20.1 percent to 7.0 percent, and green dropped from 13.4 percent to 2.2 percent. Blue’s share slipped slightly, and most other colors such as brown, beige, orange, yellow, gold and purple now each occupy less than one percent of the market. Orange is the only non‑grayscale hue to increase, though it remains rare at 0.3 percent.

The study also breaks down trends by vehicle type. Trucks are the most grayscale‑dominant segment, with 83.5 percent of late‑model trucks being white, black, gray or silver; white alone accounts for 33.6 percent of trucks. SUVs show a similar shift, moving from 43.8 percent grayscale in 1996 to 79.3 percent in 2025, with white and black each near 25 percent. Sports cars remain the most colorful category, with 36.2 percent of them featuring non‑grayscale finishes.

Analysts note that the surge in grayscale colors came largely at the expense of red and green, and that the market appears to have stabilized around an 80 percent grayscale share since 2020. This suggests that while truly neutral colors dominate, there may still be room for a modest resurgence of more vibrant options in the future. The findings matter to manufacturers, dealers and consumers because color preferences influence production planning, inventory decisions and resale values.

stories.author: sdko
stories.title: Data Processing Incidents on Inference Providers
stories.groq_label: OpenRouter offboarded three inference providers and removed 125 endpoints after security findings revealed data policy breaches
stories.groq_explain:
The blog post announces that security researchers recently discovered data compromises and policy violations at several AI inference providers. OpenRouter worked with the researchers and the affected providers to investigate the findings, confirming that OpenRouter itself suffered no breach or unauthorized data access. The investigation identified specific problems with certain providers, prompting OpenRouter to take immediate remedial actions. Three providers have been removed from the platform, and 125 model endpoints have lost Zero Data Retention eligibility. The removals include providers flagged by the researchers as well as additional endpoints taken out as a precaution. All potentially impacted customers have been notified.

OpenRouter outlines ongoing efforts to prevent future incidents. It plans to adapt the researchers’ testing methods for continuous monitoring, conduct technical verification of network paths to detect any forwarding of requests or responses to third parties, and require thorough assurances before any previously removed endpoint can regain Zero Data Retention status. The company thanks the Dragos report for its contribution and states that providers wishing to remain on OpenRouter will need to meet the higher security standards being implemented.

The post lists the security announcements that have been received from providers: a privacy notice from Novita concerning MiniMax requests, a preliminary incident report from Phala, and a security event from Together involving prompt leakage in mid‑2026. OpenRouter notes that not all affected providers have published public statements, but all users have been informed regardless. The company encourages providers to publish incident write‑ups and promises to keep the list of security announcements up to date. This matters because it demonstrates OpenRouter’s commitment to enforcing data protection policies across a rapidly evolving ecosystem of AI models and providers, and it provides transparency about how data security incidents are being addressed.

stories.author: Anon84
stories.title: The Mythology of Conscious AI
stories.groq_label: The essay argues that artificial intelligence may soon achieve consciousness, raising profound ethical and societal implications
stories.groq_explain:
The piece is an essay by neuroscientist Anil Seth, winner of the 2025 Berggruen Prize Essay Competition, titled “The Mythology of Conscious AI.” It explores the cultural, philosophical, and scientific dimensions of the question whether artificial systems can be conscious, and why that question matters.

Seth begins by noting that humanity has long been fascinated with creating artificial life, from the golem legend to Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein, and more recently through depictions such as HAL 9000, Ava in “Ex Machina,” and Klara in “Klara and the Sun.” These stories usually end badly for their creators, suggesting that the pursuit of synthetic minds carries serious risks.

He then moves to contemporary debates. In 2022 Google engineer Blake Lemoine claimed that the chatbot LaMDA was conscious, a claim that was dismissed by Google but nevertheless kept the issue alive. Prominent thinkers such as philosopher David Chalmers argue that conscious machines could appear in the near future, while AI pioneer Geoffrey Hinton believes they may already exist. A 2024 open letter from leading researchers called for serious consideration of AI welfare, indicating that many experts view machine consciousness as a question of when rather than if.

The essay stresses that how we think about conscious AI has moral, psychological, and practical consequences. If machines are or become conscious, they would acquire moral status, the capacity for suffering, and possibly rights, which would constrain our ability to shut them down. Even if they are not truly conscious, treating them as if they lack feelings can exploit human psychological vulnerabilities and distort ethical priorities. Moreover, conflating AI consciousness with human consciousness may lead us to overestimate machines and underestimate our own nature, obscuring the meaning of human experience.

In the section “The Temptations of Conscious AI,” Seth examines why people are prone to attribute consciousness to AI. He points out that humans naturally link consciousness with intelligence because we experience both, yet the two are conceptually distinct. Intelligence is defined in functional terms—solving problems, achieving goals, adapting flexibly—whereas consciousness concerns subjective experience, the “what it is like” of being an organism, a notion famously articulated by Thomas Nagel. Seth distinguishes between narrow AI, artificial general intelligence (AGI) which aims to match human cognitive abilities, and artificial superintelligence (ASI) which would surpass human comprehension. He underscores that consciousness is about “being” rather than merely “doing,” implying that advanced performance does not automatically entail subjective experience.

The essay ends abruptly while elaborating on the distinction between wakefulness and consciousness, leaving the final argument incomplete. Nonetheless, the available text makes clear that Seth’s central claim is that the mythology surrounding conscious AI shapes both our ethical treatment of emerging technologies and our understanding of what it means to be human.

stories.author: ebrahimh
stories.title: Leonida – PC Recompilation of the Xbox Version of GTA 6
stories.groq_label: Leonida is a static recompilation project that runs the Xbox Series version of GTA 6 natively on PC by translating RDNA2 shaders to SPIR‑V and reimplementing the console’s system software.
stories.groq_explain:
Leonida is a static recompilation project that enables the Xbox Series version of Grand Theft Auto VI to run natively on Windows PCs. The project works by loading the game’s original x86‑64 code directly on a PC, re‑implementing the console’s system software, and translating the console’s pre‑compiled RDNA2 GPU programs into SPIR‑V shaders for use with Vulkan. All game assets such as models, textures, and audio are read from a user’s own copy of the Xbox game package, and the project does not include the game itself, any keys, or any method for obtaining them. It merely extracts and repurposes the existing files, and it explicitly states that nothing is decrypted or bypassed, and that the generated files must remain private.

The repository documents the current status of the effort. The developers have completed the discovery and verification of the Xbox Series 1.0.2.1 game files. They have extracted and disassembled every one of the 26,503 shaders, converting them from RDNA2 to SPIR‑V and confirming their validity with spirv‑val. The conversion handles both 64‑wide wave subgroups (native on AMD hardware) and provides emulation for 32‑wide subgroups used by NVIDIA, Intel, and other GPUs. Extensive hand‑written GPU tests have been run on a wide range of graphics cards and drivers, confirming correct behavior for vertex fetching, texture sampling, compute operations, and other shader features. Models have been exported as OBJ files with proper naming and material references, and texture dictionaries and world texture pools have been extracted, though some layout decoding remains unfinished. Audio banks have been fully extracted, with Opus streams repackaged as Ogg Opus files and PCM data as WAV, while XMA2 streams are decoded using ffmpeg.

A preliminary runtime loader and import shims have been built, allowing a placeholder executable to run through the CRT startup sequence, load static data, create threads, and invoke GDK imports via the shims. The Vulkan‑backed device that mimics the Xbox D3D12 ABI is also under development; it can create queues, command lists, fences, descriptor heaps, resources, and various view types, and it supports barriers, clears, uploads, copies, resolves, and several query types. However, buffer views, root signatures, pipelines, draw calls, and swap‑chain handling have not yet been implemented, and the game does not boot or become playable at this stage.

The project provides detailed build instructions. Users must supply their own Xbox Series copy of GTA VI (version 1.0.2.1) and have about 350 GB of free disk space for intermediate files. Prerequisites include Windows 10 or 11 x64, Python 3.12 or later, .NET 8 SDK, the Vulkan SDK, LLVM 21 or newer with the AMDGPU target, Visual Studio 2022 with C++ desktop development, and the Windows SDK 10.0.26100 or newer. After cloning the repository recursively, a supplied Build.bat script locates the game files, checks for missing dependencies, and performs the compilation, placing results in a Documents\Leonida folder. The build can be paused and resumed, and the scripts support both Windows and Linux environments for certain components.

Overall, Leonida represents a technical foundation for running the Xbox version of GTA VI on PC without traditional emulation, preserving the user’s own copy of the game while reusing its assets and code. Although the project is still early and the game does not yet launch, the extensive shader translation, asset extraction, and Vulkan backend work demonstrate significant progress toward a functional PC port.

stories.author: sebaandrada
stories.title: PcapAnalyzer – self-hosted pcap analyzer with 27 problem detectors
stories.groq_label: PcapAnalyzer is a self‑hosted PCAP analyzer that runs 27 detectors to quickly identify network problems
stories.groq_explain:
PcapAnalyzer is a self‑hosted tool that analyzes network capture files (pcap or pcapng, including gzipped versions) to quickly identify faults in a network. It runs locally on the user’s machine, ensuring that captured traffic never leaves the network, and is released under the Apache 2.0 license in a beta state. The application provides twenty‑seven built‑in detectors that examine different layers of network communication. These detectors cover TCP issues such as firewall blocks, retransmissions, duplicate acknowledgments, loss, reordering, window problems, resets, and slow handshakes; path problems including PMTUD black holes, low MSS, IP fragmentation, ICMP errors, and routing loops; name and address services like unanswered or slow DNS queries, DNS errors, DHCP failures, duplicate IPs, and ARP storms; application‑level problems such as HTTP error codes, slow responses, TLS alerts, and outdated SSL/TLS versions; tunnel anomalies for IPsec, WireGuard, OpenVPN, GRE, L2TP and Teredo; and security concerns such as port scans, cleartext credential transmissions, Telnet, SMBv1, SNMP v1‑v2c, ARP spoofing, and overlapping IP fragments.

The tool also evaluates capture quality, warning when the capture itself limits the analysis, for example when frames are duplicated, traffic is seen only in one direction, packets are truncated, or connections were already open at the start of the capture. The user interface offers Wireshark‑style views with packet lists, filter support, colour coding, CSV export, expert information, tables for HTTP, DNS, DHCP and TLS, response‑time metrics and flow diagrams for each conversation.

An optional AI investigation can be enabled by supplying the user’s own Anthropic API key. The AI runs the same analysis, cites the specific packets that support each finding, and can answer follow‑up questions. A demo mode provides the full analysis without an API key, generating text from the analysis at no cost. Results can be exported as PDF reports and the interface is available in both English and Spanish with light and dark themes.

PcapAnalyzer can be started quickly using Docker and Docker Compose, which creates a random access token for the local web service. For users who prefer not to use Docker, the backend can be run with Python 3.9+ and the frontend with Node 20+, requiring tshark from Wireshark. The application listens only on localhost and must be protected by an authenticated reverse proxy if exposed to a network, because the API can access the AI account.

Privacy is emphasized: the capture is processed locally, the AI sees only encrypted metadata unless the user explicitly enables packet‑content analysis, and all data are deleted after the AI session or after a period of inactivity. No telemetry, accounts, or third‑party data collection are performed in the self‑hosted version.

The repository includes tests, a quick‑start guide, feedback instructions, and references to a technical JSON schema in Spanish. The software is free to download, with a free version hosted on Gumroad, and a live demo is available online. It matters because it enables network engineers and security analysts to diagnose problems in seconds rather than hours while keeping sensitive traffic data under their control.

stories.author: vasie
stories.title: Pandex – Official European Law for AI Agents, over MCP
stories.groq_label: Pandex provides a unified API and searchable database of EU and European national laws and court rulings for AI agents.
stories.groq_explain:
Pandex is a platform that provides official European legal documents, including national legislation, historical law versions, and highest-court rulings, formatted specifically for software applications and artificial intelligence agents. It aggregates primary legal texts straight from issuing authorities across the European Union, France, Germany, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Austria, Switzerland, Luxembourg, and the Council of Europe, with additional European countries planned for future inclusion. By unifying diverse legal systems into a single schema, the service replaces the need to write separate web scrapers for every court and jurisdiction.

The platform interfaces with existing AI development tools and provides access through a REST API and a Model Context Protocol server. It supports keyword, semantic, and hybrid search across languages, enabling users to query in one language and retrieve exact matching legal passages published in another. For compliance and legal research, Pandex tracks legislative history by maintaining past versions of legal articles alongside their effective dates, allowing software to ground answers in verified law with complete citation links.

Pandex currently manages millions of official documents, court decisions, legislative acts, searchable passages, and cross-referenced citations. It provides transparent coverage statistics for every tracked institution, explicitly reporting which legal archives are complete and noting where technical limitations, such as external bot protections or delay periods, temporarily affect full data collection.

Access to the platform starts with a free tier during its beta period, allowing up to one thousand requests per day. Commercial plans include a pay-as-you-go API option based on request volume, a founding customer program offering fixed pricing and source prioritization, and a direct feed subscription that delivers raw legal files and daily change updates for local system indexing. Pandex provides developers with a structured, reliable source of official legal data necessary for building accurate AI legal research, compliance, and monitoring tools.

stories.author: f311a
stories.title: Upload2Shell (CVE-2026-125396)
stories.groq_label: Ghostscript use after free in the Type 1 font loader (CVE 2026 125396) permits sandbox escape and remote command execution across numerous services.
stories.groq_explain:
Upload2Shell (CVE‑2026‑125396) is a critical remote‑code‑execution vulnerability discovered in Ghostscript’s Type 1 font loader. The flaw is a use‑after‑free that allows a crafted document to break out of Ghostscript’s ‑dSAFER sandbox, modify native path controls and run attacker‑chosen commands inside the rendering process. Because Ghostscript is commonly invoked by print, email, upload and preview pipelines, the vulnerability can be reached through many downstream services.

The researchers first identified a path out of the ‑dSAFER boundary on 27 July 2026. By 30 July they demonstrated that a signed‑out request for a malicious file could reach Ghostscript in Google’s document rendering pipeline, and they supplied a production‑grade proof to Google. In August WordPress Core was shown to expose the renderer to users with Author privileges and to Contributors granted the upload_files capability, leading to a separate fix (CVE‑2026‑65640). The upstream Artifex bug tracker received a report (Bug 709684) on 2 September, and a Ghostscript release (10.08.0) was made available by 9 September.

Further production‑level findings were confirmed in other services. A Dropbox document‑processing route, Debian’s CUPS IPP service, Roundcube’s thumbnail generation, Plesk Obsidian’s Roundcube integration, the Essential Addons for Elementor widget, Forminator’s PDF form handling, Mayan EDMS’s document inbox, DokuWiki’s ImageMagick backend, MediaWiki’s PdfHandler, and ResourceSpace’s preview worker all exhibited remote command execution when processing malicious inputs that passed through Ghostscript. Each vendor was contacted in mid‑September and the reports were logged with timestamps.

Debian published a security update for Ghostscript in its unstable branch on 12 September, followed by a Debian 13 security update on 25 September. The same month Debian Security released a stable‑security update (10.05.1~dfsg‑1+deb13u3) marking the issue fixed. Ubuntu’s USN‑8949‑1 on 21 October incorporated the Ghostscript fix for seven Ubuntu releases, including Pro and Legacy branches. Roundcube released a hardening update on 19 October to restrict unsafe image types before ImageMagick conversion (CVE‑2026‑114727). Google mitigated its production path on 9 November, and a CVE identifier was assigned on 9 November, with the public CVE‑2026‑125396 entry published on 10 November.

The timeline concludes with an ongoing “rolling publication” of case studies, proofs and vendor responses, and a note that any additional print filters, thumbnailers or document preview components that invoke Ghostscript could become future attack vectors. The vulnerability matters because it provides pre‑authentication remote code execution across a wide array of widely deployed services, potentially compromising servers running Debian, Ubuntu, Google Cloud, WordPress sites, email platforms and many open‑source web applications. The coordinated disclosure and rapid patching across the ecosystem illustrate the broad impact of a single low‑level flaw in a foundational image‑processing library.

stories.author: k__
stories.title: Inkling-2-Mini in 5.4 GB Memory
stories.groq_label: LookAtMyQuant compresses Inkling-2-Mini to 5.4 GB at 1.63 bits per weight while preserving most of its performance.
stories.groq_explain:
The page describes LookAtMyQuant, a quantization compiler that evaluates the impact of compressing each stored element of a model on its output and selects coding schemes so the entire model fits a size budget with minimal degradation. The tool is released under the MIT license and the methods and results are documented on the site.

LookAtMyQuant 2 is demonstrated on several models. For Qwen3.5‑4B it reduces the model to 1.23 GB, about 2.3 bits per weight, while still solving 330 of 540 exact‑answer math problems. This is comparable to Prism ML’s Bonsai 2 Ternary 4B, which solves 328 problems at a similar size, but the original Qwen3.5‑4B solves 359. The KL divergence of the quantized model on held‑out text is 0.45 nats versus 0.59 for Bonsai. The approach combines post‑training quantization with trellis codes, calibration on the model’s own math solutions (giving digit tokens ten times more weight), Fisher‑information‑based bit allocation per row, and 4 000 steps of distillation where each layer is re‑quantized once from the original weights. The entire process costs roughly $34 of GPU time. The resulting 1.23 GB file is packaged for the Apple Silicon runtime.

Applying the same recipe to Qwen3.8‑27B compresses it from 53.7 GB to 7.2 GB (2.1 bits per weight) while retaining full performance on the 540 math benchmark (401 correct answers) and surpassing a competing Unsloth GGUF of the same size on HumanEval, MMLU and GSM8K. A 4‑bit DSpine drafter (1.02 GB) is also provided, which roughly doubles decode speed on math and code on Apple silicon.

The section titled “Inkling‑2‑Mini in 5.4 GB and 8.9 GB” details the compression of the 26.4 B physical / 5.4 B active 3‑times‑looped mixture‑of‑experts model from thinkingmachines/Inkling‑2‑Mini. Using the same compiler and a proximal fine‑tuning method (SQYFR), the model is reduced to 5.38 GB (1.63 bits per weight) and to 8.87 GB (2.69 bits per weight). Compression employs 4 KB SRAM hashed block‑vector trellis codes, row trellis codes, and a floor on the tail language‑model head bucket. Evaluations against the BF16 teacher model on GSM8K (200 test items) and HumanEval (164 problems) show that the 5.38 GB version achieves 134 correct GSM8K answers (67 % of the teacher) and 60 correct HumanEval solutions (36.6 %). The 8.87 GB version matches the teacher on GSM8K with 148 correct answers (74 %) and improves KL divergence compared with several Unsloth GGUF variants. At 5.38 GB the model outperforms a 9.14 GB Unsloth model on both GSM8K and HumanEval while being 41 % smaller. At 8.87 GB it matches the BF16 teacher on GSM8K and reduces KL by more than twofold on English/chat/code and by 29.6 % across 13 languages relative to the Unsloth baseline.

Performance on Apple silicon is reported for both compressed sizes. The 5.4 GB model decodes at about 73 tokens per second serially and a median of 125 tokens per second, with higher rates for math, reasoning and code, and a prefill speed of roughly 1 037 tokens per second using 5.83 GB of RAM. The 8.9 GB model decodes at about 63 tokens per second serially and a median of 101 tokens per second, with a prefill speed of 838 tokens per second using 9.32 GB RAM.

Installation instructions are provided for Apple silicon: installing the runtime package via pip from the GitHub repository, which brings in mlx, mlx‑lm, numpy and huggingface‑hub without needing PyTorch. The lamq command line tool can generate or chat with any supported model, optionally using a drafter, and accepts various flags for prompt handling, temperature, mode, and output format. The page also shows how to load a model programmatically with the runtime_mlx Python module, returning a model and tokenizer compatible with mlx_lm generation functions.

Overall, the page presents a quantization framework that achieves substantial size reductions for large language models while preserving or even improving task performance, and offers ready‑to‑use Apple silicon binaries and tooling for developers.

stories.author: andsoitis
stories.title: Jensen Huang's fall is bad news for Silicon Valley's accelerationists

stories.author: valyala
stories.title: PostgreSQL Extensions in Go
stories.groq_label: gopgext enables building PostgreSQL extensions directly from Go code with TinyGo, automatically generating the necessary C glue, control files, and SQL integration.
stories.groq_explain:
The page describes gopgext, a tool that lets developers create PostgreSQL extensions using plain Go code compiled with TinyGo. By adding a //gopgext:function comment to a Go function, the tool generates the necessary C glue code, installation script and control file so that the function appears as a SQL callable function inside PostgreSQL. The project is experimental; it warns that generated code or the Go runtime may crash the server, corrupt data, or change without notice, and it should not be used in production.

The documentation explains that a typical gopgext project consists of ordinary Go source files. The Go standard library is largely supported, including packages such as fmt, regexp, encoding/json, crypto, as well as language features like maps, generics, iterators, defer and recover. Go types are automatically mapped to PostgreSQL types, covering strings, numeric types, arrays, NULLs, sets, rows, timestamps, UUIDs and JSON. Users can also define custom data and composite types in Go.

SQL execution is performed through PostgreSQL’s Server Programming Interface (SPI); functions can return errors with proper SQLSTATE codes, log messages, read configuration settings and respond to query cancellations. Beyond simple functions, gopgext can generate triggers, aggregate functions, GiST, GIN, SP‑GiST and BRIN operator classes, custom index access methods, foreign data wrappers and query hooks. The tool has been validated against PostgreSQL’s contrib modules such as pgcrypto, hstore, pg_stat_statements and cube, passing upstream regression tests.

The page notes that multiple Go extensions can be loaded into a single backend safely. PostgreSQL errors never unwind through Go frames, and results are copied into PostgreSQL’s memory management. An example is given where a Hello function returns a greeting and a Shout function converts a string to uppercase or returns an error for an empty input. The tutorial shows how to initialize a module, build the shared library, create the extension in psql and call the function.

Finally, it mentions a sibling project, gokm, which builds Linux kernel modules from Go using a similar approach: a custom TinyGo target, a host‑specific C runtime compiled by the host’s build system, and generated glue code. The overall significance is that gopgext opens the possibility of writing PostgreSQL extensions in Go, leveraging Go’s language features and libraries while integrating tightly with PostgreSQL’s extension framework.

stories.author: Bluestein
stories.title: Verification files for the Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis
stories.groq_label: Lean verification shows the Riemann Hypothesis proof compiles error free and all five headline theorems are validated using only three standard axioms.
stories.groq_explain:
The page presents the verification files for a Lean formal proof of the Riemann Hypothesis that was announced on 20 November 2026. The proof, attributed to Andrew Sutherland at MIT, was checked using Claude Code and the results were posted on 21 November 2026. The page lists a series of automated checks that confirm the correctness of the Lean source, the absence of unexpected axioms, and the ability of multiple independent kernels to accept the exported proof.

All 175,187 modules of the Lean source compile without errors using Lean version 4.33.1 and Mathlib version 4.33.1. The five main theorems depend only on the three standard axioms propext, Classical.choice and Quot.sound, and no additional axioms are introduced outside the Lean core. The environment contains only the expected 15 axioms located in the Init Mathlib files. A full replay of every module through the Lean kernel succeeds with zero rejections. Independent Rust‑based kernel nanoda verifies the complete export in under thirty minutes on 80 threads. The default Lean kernel and a paranoid kernel are still running single‑threaded checks. The lake comparator, running with Lean version 4.36.0, has already passed statement comparison and axiom checks for one run, while the con‑leche kernel accepts all 1,468,418 declarations in verified mode and confirms that each of the five theorems is justified by the solution. The con‑leche compare mode also matches the challenge file against the solution for all five theorems. The lean4lean tool processes all modules, with five modules requiring a higher step limit to complete.

The five verified theorems are the statements that constitute the Riemann Hypothesis and its generalization to Dirichlet L‑functions. The first theorem states that every non‑trivial zero of the Riemann zeta function has real part one half. The second theorem restates the same claim in the author’s own wording, which Lean recognizes as definitionally equal to the first. The third theorem asserts that for any modulus N and any Dirichlet character χ, the associated L‑function is non‑zero when the real part of s exceeds one half, except for the trivial character at its pole. The fourth theorem says that any zero of a Dirichlet L‑function within the critical strip must lie on the critical line. The fifth theorem restricts this result to primitive characters, which is the usual formulation of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L‑functions.

The scope of the verification is limited to Dirichlet L‑functions; Dedekind zeta functions, Hecke L‑functions and more general automorphic L‑functions were not part of the checked statements. As an additional arithmetic check that does not rely on Mathlib’s definition of the zeta function, the proof was combined with an independent formalization of Robin’s and Lagarias’s criteria. This combination yields two unconditional inequalities about the divisor‑sum function, demonstrating that the formal proof can be linked with other number‑theoretic results in the same Lean environment.

Overall, the page documents a comprehensive series of automated verifications that confirm the Lean proof compiles, respects the intended axioms, and is accepted by multiple independent verification tools, thereby providing strong evidence that the formalized statements of the Riemann Hypothesis and its Dirichlet generalization have been successfully encoded in Lean.

stories.author: reverseblade2
stories.title: Show HN: Zero C#, Power of C# without any GC
stories.groq_label: Zero C# compiles C# to native binaries without a runtime or garbage collector while preserving language features
stories.groq_explain:
Zero C# is a fork of the bflat compiler that turns C# source code directly into a small native executable, eliminating the need for a .NET runtime, garbage collector, or any additional installation on the target machine. The project preserves the full C# syntax, type checking, generics and newer language features such as C# 15 unions, extension members, default interface methods, records, tuples, anonymous types, lambdas and query operators. The only runtime service that is removed is automatic memory management; memory is allocated from arenas that are freed in a single operation when the programmer decides. A lightweight library supplies string handling, collections, input and output that operate on these arenas, allowing code such as stack‑allocated buffers and direct writes to output buffers without creating temporary heap objects.

The same C# source can be compiled for Linux, macOS, Windows, WebAssembly, and even DOS on a 386 processor. Sample builds show hello‑world binaries that range from about ten kilobytes on Windows to roughly forty kilobytes on Linux, with each binary depending only on the platform’s C library. The build process works from Linux or macOS and can target macOS native binaries, Windows executables (tested under Wine), WASI modules that run with wasmtime, and 386 DOS programs that run under emulators like Bochs.

Because there is no garbage collector, certain runtime behaviors change. The “new” operator never frees memory; instead, arenas allocate all needed objects and release them together. Exceptions are not caught; throwing an exception terminates the program, so error handling is expressed with union types. Reflection and async features are unavailable, and the type system does not retain full type names at runtime. Collections such as lists and dictionaries are provided as arena‑based structures, and output functions format directly into buffers to avoid temporary strings.

Zero C# includes documentation that explains the memory model, string handling, collection usage, and the updated memory‑safety rules that make pointer creation safe. A short tutorial walks new users through installing the forked compiler, building a first program, running it on DOS, and completing a quiz‑style tutorial that demonstrates input, output, error handling and arena management. The project demonstrates that C# can be used for ultra‑small native programs while keeping most of the language’s expressive power, opening possibilities for low‑resource environments and platforms where a full .NET runtime would be impractical.

stories.author: g-b-r
stories.title: Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis
stories.groq_label: Levent Alpöge’s 17 million line Lean library is declared a verified proof of the Riemann Hypothesis by the Lean and Mathlib communities
stories.groq_explain:
The page announces a joint statement from the Lean and Mathlib communities, endorsed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative, declaring that a formal proof of the Riemann Hypothesis has been completed in the Lean theorem‑proving system. On 20 November 2026, Levent Alpöge released a library containing a proof that spans roughly 17 million lines of Lean code. The announcement asserts full confidence in the correctness of this proof and outlines the reasons for that confidence.

According to the statement, the code depends only on Mathlib, the standard library for Lean. Over the course of a day, many members of the Lean and Mathlib communities compiled the library without errors, reproducing the same raw proof export file. A separate file that isolates the hypothesis statement imports only Mathlib, and two independent tools—comparator and con‑leche –compare—verified that the theorem proved by Alpöge matches exactly the Mathlib definition of the Riemann Hypothesis.

The raw proof export has been examined by several proof‑checking programs, including Lean’s own kernel and the external checkers con‑leche and con‑ron, as well as additional checkers contributed by third parties in various programming languages. Both con‑leche and con‑ron come with formal proofs, relative to set theory, that they cannot accept a false proof, addressing any concerns about possible flaws in Lean’s logical foundations. The verification process was performed on an inert export of the proof, isolated from any potentially malicious code in the source files.

The announcement concludes by thanking the community for the verification effort and expresses anticipation for further mathematical work that will explain the new ideas introduced in this proof. An extensive overview of the verification is said to be available at a MIT URL.

stories.author: soheilpro
stories.title: My monitor was cutting my download speed by 75%
stories.groq_label: Connecting the USB‑C Ethernet adapter through the Studio Display XDR limited download speeds to about 600 Mbps due to the monitor’s handling of flow control and driver issues.
stories.groq_explain:
The author discovered that connecting a 2.5 Gbps symmetric internet line through a Studio Display XDR dramatically reduced download speed to about 600 Mbps while upload remained near the full 2.4 Gbps. The problem began after moving all wired connections to the monitor’s single‑cable setup, which includes a UGREEN USB‑C to 2.5 Gbps Ethernet adapter plugged into the display’s hub.

Testing showed that the adapter, the router (UniFi Dream Router 7), and the Ethernet cable all performed correctly when the adapter was connected directly to the MacBook Pro. Speed tests and iperf3 runs gave over 2 Gbps in both directions. When the adapter was routed through the display, download speed dropped and occasional ping losses occurred, indicating that the monitor’s hub was discarding frames before macOS could see them.

The adapter uses a Realtek RTL8156B chip that macOS drives with its generic USB networking driver. Installing Realtek’s own driver increased download speed to about 1.1 Gbps but still fell short of the 2.5 Gbps capability, suggesting the issue was not solely the monitor.

The key factor turned out to be Ethernet flow control. Without flow control the receiver (the adapter inside the monitor) drops frames it cannot process quickly enough. Enabling flow control on the UniFi router allowed the sender to pause and buffer data, raising download speed to roughly 2 Gbps. The author notes that keeping flow control always on can add latency to other devices such as a gaming PC, so it may need to be disabled selectively.

Further investigation with a Linux box sending steady UDP traffic revealed that the RTL8156B could only pass about 168 000 frames per second (roughly 2 Gbps) to the Mac before dropping packets. The drop point corresponded to the adapter’s internal limit of handling four‑kilobyte bursts, whereas the Mac’s USB‑3 SSD controller uses larger 16‑packet bursts, allowing higher throughput. The monitor’s Thunderbolt hub adds about 7.6 µs of latency per transaction, and sending a 4 KB packet takes roughly 8.2 µs, together limiting the effective outbound speed.

In summary, the Studio Display’s USB‑C hub introduces a bottleneck for high‑speed Ethernet traffic because the Realtek adapter’s small burst size and lack of flow control cause frame loss. Enabling flow control mitigates the problem but may affect latency for other devices. The post highlights the importance of understanding hub limitations and flow‑control settings when using the display as a networking hub, especially for users with multi‑gigabit internet connections.

stories.author: gdgghhhhh
stories.title: RCE in Gnupg
stories.groq_label: Critical double free vulnerability in GPGME identified as CVE 2026 129975 is fixed in version 2.3.1 and users should update immediately
stories.groq_explain:
The announcement, authored by Werner Koch, informs recipients that a new version of the GPGME library, version 2.3.1, is now available. The release addresses a critical security vulnerability that existed in all earlier versions of GPGME. The flaw is triggered by an OpenPGP key containing an exceptionally long user identifier, which can cause a double‑free condition in the library’s handling of status lines and key listings. Because the pointer to the newly allocated buffer is not correctly updated when the function returns early, the old memory can be freed a second time later, potentially allowing an attacker to exfiltrate data and possibly achieve remote code execution.

The vulnerability is identified internally as T8557 and has been assigned CVE‑2026‑129975. It was discovered by Johan Carlsson and reported to the GnuPG project on 12 November 2026. A coordinated disclosure was originally planned for 25 November 2026, but due to a separate issue with GitLab’s Ruby2Shell bug, the disclosure was moved up to 20 November 2026.

All software that incorporates GPGME versions prior to 2.3.0—whether linked as a shared library, DLL, or statically—are affected. This includes popular packages such as Gpg4win, GnuPG Desktop, GnuPG VS‑Desktop, many mail and XMPP clients, Samba, and applications distributed via Flatpak. Users are urged to upgrade to GPGME 2.3.1 immediately. The announcement provides several options: replace the shared library with the updated version, obtain the patched DLL from the new Gpg4win release, or rebuild statically linked binaries against the new library. A patch for older versions is attached for those unable to upgrade, and it is noted that GPGMEPP and GPGMEQT do not need updating.

The changelog for 2.3.1, released on 19 November 2026, adds new algorithm constants (GPGME_PK_MLKEM, GPGME_PK_MLDSA, and GPGME_PK_DLTHM) and fixes the double‑free bug. Version 2.3.0 was never publicly released. The announcement also includes download links for the source tarball and its signature, checksums for verification, and information about Debian‑style packages and a new Windows installer (Gpg4win 5.1.2) that bundles the fixed library, the Kleopatra GUI, and a PDF reader.

Finally, the message lists the signing keys used to certify the releases, provides URLs for integrity checking, and directs replies to the gnupg‑users mailing list, emphasizing that this is an announcement‑only distribution. The release is significant because the vulnerability could allow attackers to compromise a wide range of applications that rely on GPGME for cryptographic operations. Prompt updating mitigates the risk of data leakage and potential remote code execution.

stories.author: sammatilda
stories.title: Clojure will affect the way you think about programming (2017)
stories.groq_label: Clojure’s Lisp heritage and emphasis on immutable data structures fundamentally reshape how programmers approach code.
stories.groq_explain:
The article argues that Clojure is an ideal language to learn next because it reshapes how programmers think about software. The author begins by noting that exposure to diverse languages is essential for programming growth, but limited time makes the choice of language critical. Clojure, first released in 2007, is described as a modern Lisp that unifies insights from many earlier languages into a coherent whole, making it especially effective at expanding a programmer’s mindset.

As a member of the Lisp family, Clojure brings several distinctive features. It is primarily a dynamic language with optional typing, encouraging developers to work with built‑in data structures such as lists, maps, and vectors rather than relying on traditional object‑oriented models. Higher‑order functions are central, and constructs like reducers and transducers demonstrate powerful function composition. The language’s uniform syntax and full macro system force programmers to treat code as data, a perspective the author claims leads to deeper insights and creative solutions. Clojure also includes a CSP‑style concurrency library (core.async) implemented with macros, and it promotes REPL‑driven development where code and tests evolve interactively.

The author stresses Clojure’s pragmatism, citing the experience of its creator Rich Hickey. Hickey’s talks emphasize simplicity emerging from complexity, a philosophy reflected in Clojure’s design and its supportive community. The article highlights Clojure’s modern tooling, such as persistent data structures that were only researched in the 1990s, and a rich ecosystem of libraries suited to contemporary programming tasks.

Data processing is presented as a key strength. Clojure’s pervasive sequence abstractions, lazy evaluation, and immutable collections make it natural to express SQL‑like pipelines directly in code. An example from the book *Clojure Applied* shows a function that filters, transforms, groups, and reduces a collection of shopping carts using only built‑in functions and the thread‑macro, producing readable, efficient, and potentially parallelizable code. The language also offers clojure.spec for describing and validating nested data structures, providing optional type‑safety, while core.typed offers a more statically‑typed alternative.

Although Lisp traditions have not always embraced object‑orientation, Clojure includes a set of OO‑like features that the author describes as powerful, suggesting a balanced approach to OOP within a functional, data‑centric paradigm.

The article ends abruptly while discussing Clojure’s object‑orientation, but the overall message is clear: learning Clojure is likely to change a programmer’s conceptual toolbox by exposing them to Lisp’s macro system, immutable data, lazy sequences, and a pragmatic design philosophy, making it a valuable addition to any developer’s skill set.

stories.author: mooreds
stories.title: Sir Brian May adds new dimension to Hera asteroid
stories.groq_label: Sir Brian May produced stereoscopic imagery of the Didymos asteroid from Hera mission data, revealing detailed 3D features.
stories.groq_explain:
The article reports that Sir Brian May, the astrophysicist and guitarist of the band Queen, has produced a stereoscopic image of the asteroid Didymos using data from ESA’s Hera planetary‑defence mission. The two pictures were taken on 6 November while Hera orbited the Didymos system at a distance of 29.7 km with a resolution of 2.8 metres per pixel. By pairing the adjacent frames, May created a three‑dimensional view that highlights the sharp, smooth equatorial ridge of Didymos in contrast with the rough, rock‑strewn terrain elsewhere. Hera’s principal investigator Patrick Michel remarks that the stereo pairs make observers feel as if they are present at the asteroid despite the 197 million‑kilometre distance, adding scientific value to the striking visual effect.

The stereoscopic image was assembled together with colleague Claudia Manzoni and relies on the Asteroid Framing Camera, whose principal investigator is Jean‑Baptiste Vincent of the German Aerospace Center. The article explains that the slight differences between the two frames mimic human binocular vision, and it describes several ways to view the 3‑D picture: with red‑blue glasses, by crossing the eyes, by focusing into infinity, or with a dedicated viewer such as the OWL stereoscope designed by May and sold by the London Stereoscopic Company.

The piece also places the image in the broader context of the Hera mission. After NASA’s DART spacecraft deliberately collided with Dimorphos, the small moonlet of Didymos, in 2022 to alter its orbit, Hera has arrived to conduct a close‑up “crash‑scene investigation” of the binary system. The mission aims to collect detailed data that will turn the DART experiment into a well‑understood and repeatable planetary‑defence technique. A livestream scheduled for 25 November will broadcast the first close‑up images of the transformed asteroid, and readers are invited to follow the event on ESA WebTV or YouTube and to subscribe to ESA’s newsletter.

The significance of the story lies in the novel three‑dimensional visualisation of a near‑Earth asteroid, which enhances scientific analysis of its shape and surface features, supports the assessment of impact outcomes, and showcases public outreach by linking a celebrated musician with cutting‑edge space research.

stories.author: CharlesW
stories.title: NINLIVE: The Nine Inch Nails live archive

Access to streaming and the ability to save favorite shows requires logging in with a Discord account. There is a particular call for photographers who would like to have their work linked on the archive. The maintainer also mentions ongoing work converting analog sources such as cassette tapes, VHS recordings and DAT tapes to digital format, and offers to help others with similar transfers.

Recent activity is highlighted with dates from the past few weeks, and the site notes that it also covers side projects and related musical paths associated with Nine Inch Nails. Overall, NINLIVE serves as a comprehensive, community‑driven repository for live performance material, providing both a historical record and a modern streaming experience for fans.

stories.author: rafaelc
stories.title: Pill to treat pancreatic cancer hailed as 'biggest breakthrough in decades'
stories.groq_label: Daraxonrasib, a KRAS inhibiting pill, shrank or eliminated pancreatic tumors in most trial patients, representing the most significant breakthrough in decades
stories.groq_explain:
The article reports on a new oral drug called daraxonrasib that has shown remarkable results in a clinical trial for patients with advanced pancreatic cancer that has spread to other parts of the body. In the study, tumours stopped growing in about 90 percent of the 61 participants, more than 60 percent experienced tumour shrinkage or disappearance, and roughly one in twelve patients (about 8 percent) had tumours become undetectable on CT scans. After a year of treatment, 76.6 percent of patients were still alive, compared with the typical 40‑45 percent survival rate for patients receiving chemotherapy alone.

The trial participants were followed for an average of 18 months; some showed no cancer recurrence during that period. Although doctors caution that the pill cannot yet be called a cure and the duration of disease control remains uncertain, the findings are described as the closest approach to a cure seen in pancreatic cancer for decades. Dr Wungki Park, who presented the data at a European oncology symposium in Barcelona, highlighted the unprecedented depth of tumour responses and the near‑doubling of disease‑control duration.

Daraxonrasib works as a KRAS inhibitor, targeting specific mutations that drive tumour growth in most pancreatic cancers. Because similar KRAS mutations occur in many other cancers, researchers are hopeful the drug could eventually be applied to a broader range of tumours. Cancer Research UK’s chief executive, Michelle Mitchell, called the results the biggest leap forward in pancreatic‑cancer treatment in decades, while noting that further trials are needed before the drug can be considered for the NHS. The breakthrough matters because pancreatic cancer has the lowest survival rate of common cancers in the UK and globally, with half of patients dying within three months of diagnosis and only about three percent surviving five years after metastasis. Any therapy that can significantly extend survival or induce remission could change the outlook for a disease that has been notoriously difficult to treat.

stories.author: jasondavies
stories.title: Inkling 2 Mini
stories.groq_label: Inkling 2 Mini is a looped transformer with 26.4 B parameters that achieves leading performance among sub‑100 B open‑weight models while running on consumer laptops
stories.groq_explain:
Inkling 2 Mini is a new open‑weight language model released by Thinking Machines. It is designed to be fast and powerful while fitting on a typical laptop, with a total parameter count of 26.4 billion, of which only 3.4 billion are active at any time. The model uses a looped transformer architecture, running the middle layers three times for each token. This looping lets the model perform more reasoning steps without producing longer output, improving answer quality on tasks that require deep thought such as agentic coding.

The developers report that Inkling 2 Mini leads every open‑weight model under 100 billion parameters on benchmarks like DeepSWE v1.1 (48.2 percent) and Vals Index v2.2 (46.5 percent). It also matches the performance of much larger models on certain kernel‑optimization and code‑generation tests, trailing only the proprietary Qwen 3.8‑27B on a few tasks. The model’s decoding speed approaches a theoretical ceiling of 614 GB/s when using BF16 weights with batch size one, and its memory footprint of roughly 20 GB allows it to run on consumer laptops and desktop AI machines.

A variable‑loop variant was released alongside the main model to study the effects of looping depth. Experiments showed that increasing the number of passes from one to three more than doubled the no‑chain‑of‑thought execution time (from 16 to 37 seconds) and continued to improve performance on serial‑reasoning benchmarks even beyond the training loop count. More loops shortened the generated chain‑of‑thought but kept it readable, and looping did not increase the model’s propensity for agentic sabotage.

Most of Inkling 2 Mini’s weights are stored natively in NVFP4 format, with the final four layers in MXFP8. The team demonstrated the model’s portability by running it offline on a MacBook Pro (M5 Pro, 48 GB RAM) during a flight, where it built a playable flight simulator in a few minutes. The model is available with open weights and can be accessed for inference and customization through the Tinker platform.

In terms of capabilities, Inkling 2 Mini excels at long‑horizon, agentic work and outperforms comparable open‑weight models on agentic coding benchmarks such as DeepSWE and SWE‑bench Pro v2. Its factuality score (AA‑Omniscience) is comparable to other models of similar size, confirming that looping improves reasoning without adding new knowledge. The model compensates for limited knowledge by efficiently using external search and tool use, leading open‑weight models of its size on benchmarks that involve browsing, deep search QA, and multi‑modal tool use. Overall, Inkling 2 Mini offers a compelling combination of reasoning depth, speed, and low hardware requirements, making advanced AI research more accessible to those without large‑scale compute resources.

stories.author: notfried
stories.title: And yet, it moves
stories.groq_label: Anthropic’s alleged proof of the Riemann Hypothesis marks a shift toward AI-driven breakthroughs, echoing Galileo’s legacy while questioning humanity’s future role in discovery
stories.groq_explain:
The author begins by describing a recent experience watching a new Broadway musical about Galileo, noting that it feels like a “Hamilton knock‑off” with modern rock songs, a stubborn protagonist, familial conflict, and historical themes. The performance is praised for its strong actors, especially Joy Woods as Galileo’s daughter Virginia and Jeremy Kushnier as Bishop Barberini, and receives a personal rating of 8.5 out of 10. The writer argues that historical musicals succeed in making the often “insane” aspects of history more vivid, comparing Hamilton’s revolutionary political narrative to Galileo’s scientific breakthrough that expanded humanity’s view of the universe.

The piece then shifts to the claim that the AI company Anthropic has solved the Riemann Hypothesis, a long‑standing unsolved problem in mathematics. The author reflects on how such a solution could have sparked celebrations comparable to major scientific milestones, but instead the reaction feels muted and bittersweet. The proof’s origin in an “inscrutable silicon mind” rather than a human mathematician leaves the author feeling that the achievement is less a triumph of humanity and more a sign that humans are ceding discovery to machines.

Drawing a parallel to Galileo’s forced recantation and his famous alleged remark “Eppur si muove” (“And yet, it moves”), the writer contends that truth exists independently of authority and that humanity’s role in uncovering truth is waning. The author expresses a melancholy longing for progress to halt, fearing that future discoveries will only occur when no one else has already delegated the question to powerful AI. The essay concludes with a resigned affirmation that, despite this, the world continues to move forward. The article uses the Galileo narrative to explore the cultural impact of AI‑driven breakthroughs and to question the future of human intellectual agency.

stories.author: facundo_olano
stories.title: DreamCoder: Coding harness and IDE from the author of Mastering Emacs
stories.groq_label: DreamCoder is an AI-powered coding harness featuring a browser‑based tiling window manager, released after fifteen months of development.
stories.groq_explain:
The author announces the release of DreamCoder, an AI‑driven coding harness and integrated development environment that he has been developing for fifteen months. After experimenting with Claude Code in mid‑2025 and finding its terminal‑only interface limiting, he set out to create a more capable tool. DreamCoder is described as a “frontier coding harness” that runs in a browser, works on all three major platforms, and features a tiling window manager rather than the typical sidebar‑and‑chat UI of most current AI coding assistants. The author emphasizes that the new harness is designed to avoid the frustrations of copying and pasting multi‑line code in a terminal and to provide a richer, more flexible environment for serious programmers.

Before detailing the product, the article provides a brief historical overview linking Emacs, LISP, and early AI research. It recounts John McCarthy’s 1950s effort to build the Advice Taker, his creation of the LISP language with its M‑expressions and S‑expressions, and the subsequent development of the first LISP interpreter by Steve Russell. The narrative explains how S‑expressions became the core of LISP and how the language’s ability to treat code as data enabled symbolic reasoning, a foundation for modern AI work. The piece notes that while M‑expressions faded, they survive in environments like Mathematica, and reflects on McCarthy’s later comments about LISP’s strengths and perceived disadvantages.

The article ends abruptly while illustrating a simple symbolic representation of navigation facts, suggesting that the full explanation of DreamCoder’s capabilities and usage may continue beyond the provided excerpt. Overall, the post serves both as a product announcement for DreamCoder and as a contextual essay on the historical roots of AI programming tools in LISP and Emacs.

stories.author: jasondavies
stories.title: Hurried Announcement: Alessandro Masullo GRH
stories.groq_label: Alessandro Masullo's draft proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis is being released urgently for community review.
stories.groq_explain: The post is a brief, urgent notice posted on November 20, 2026 by a member of the American Mathematical Society’s Executive Committee and Board of Trustees. The author says they are currently at an AMS meeting but needed to share a draft of a proposed proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH) by Alessandro Masullo. According to the announcement, the proof has been examined for months by Brian Conrad, who has provided extensive feedback that is being incorporated, and the reviewers consider it promising. The author notes that the work is entirely human‑produced, with no AI involvement, and that the plan was originally to bring Masullo to Stanford for a year to polish the manuscript before a formal announcement. Because of the perceived importance, the author wants to release the current draft now so that the mathematical community can review it, formalize any details, and fill any small gaps that may appear. The post emphasizes confidence in Conrad’s judgment and expresses hope that the proof will ultimately be correct. No actual mathematical content or the draft itself is included in the page; only a generic WordPress footer appears after the announcement. The message matters because a valid proof of GRH would resolve one of the most significant open problems in analytic number theory, with far‑reaching consequences throughout mathematics.

stories.author: QueensGambit
stories.title: We promoted developers into architects without informing them
stories.groq_label: Architects must push back on requirements that harm performance and choose logging approaches that balance speed, security, and data needs.
stories.groq_explain:
The article recounts a recent incident in which a colleague added extensive logging to a Google Forms add‑on in order to monitor new installations. By trying to capture the user’s email, then the user ID, and finally falling back to an error message, the code made several API calls on every install. Because the logging ran before the welcome screen, the screen took about fifteen seconds to load, creating a serious performance problem.

The author explains that a senior developer or architect would have approached the requirement differently. Instead of attempting to fetch personal data synchronously, they would have logged only a timestamp, informing the marketing team that follow‑up email addresses could not be obtained at install time. If the marketing team needed the email, the architect would have shown the welcome screen first and logged the email or ID asynchronously, while ensuring that any server calls respected security constraints and did not require unauthenticated payloads.

The piece then critiques AI code generators, noting that while they can produce functional code, they lack awareness of scale, user volume, and the trade‑offs between performance and security. AI tends to follow the literal requirements without pushing back, which can lead to slow, insecure, or overly complex implementations. The author argues that the correct approach is to specify architectural constraints first, design the data model, and then let AI generate code within those limits. Whenever a requirement would change the architecture, the tool should ask for confirmation rather than silently rewriting it.

A broader point is made about the changing role of developers. Many developers who excel at coding are being moved into architect positions without clear guidance. Their new responsibilities include challenging unrealistic requirements, designing data models, constraining AI‑generated code, and reviewing implementations for performance and maintainability. The author stresses that while the hands‑on coding work may be increasingly automated, the need for architectural oversight remains, and developers should adapt by learning to think like architects. The article serves as a warning and a call to action for developers who have been “promoted” to architects without being told.

stories.author: ankitvgupta
stories.title: Vibecoding an Inference Chip
stories.groq_label: A large language model was successfully deployed on an FPGA using AI coding agents, reaching real‑time inference speeds.
stories.groq_explain:
The author recounts how they used AI coding agents to program an FPGA to run a large‑language‑model inference engine, a process they refer to as “vibe‑coding.” Starting with only a basic understanding of field‑programmable gate arrays—reconfigurable chips that can be programmed at the hardware level for potential performance gains—they set out to see whether modern large language models could handle the low‑level C++ and Verilog work required for such a task.  

Using AWS F2 instances that provide FPGA hardware with 16 GB of high‑bandwidth memory, the author asked Codex to reserve an instance and began an extended experiment that combined automated agent work with occasional human prompts. The goal was to run a ternary‑weight model, a design from DeepGrove that is suited to memory‑limited environments and already performs well on macOS.  

Over several days the AI agents, running under the Conductor orchestration framework, generated roughly three million lines of code and parsed thirty million lines of output. They iteratively refined the design, moving from a baseline implementation to a version that achieved a thirty‑three‑fold speed increase, reaching 213 tokens per second compared with the initial performance. Key optimizations included a head loader that accessed both memory banks simultaneously, a prefetch policy, timing fixes, and a modest reduction in clock frequency to avoid random faults.  

The author emphasizes that most prompts to the agents were simple, such as urging the model to be more creative or to aim for a two‑fold speedup, with occasional domain‑specific suggestions like speculative decoding or porting CPU‑bound code to the FPGA. Both the Astra and Opus agents performed adequately, and the human contribution—particularly a prompt supplied by the DeepGrove founders—provided the most useful guidance, steering the agents away from overly time‑consuming tasks like cycle‑accurate simulation.  

The experiment cost about ten thousand dollars in Claude and OpenAI token usage, demonstrating that large token budgets can enable extensive autoresearch loops without prohibitive expense. The author notes that even without deep personal experience in C++ or Verilog, the AI‑driven workflow made the project feasible, highlighting a new paradigm where developers can leverage powerful language models to explore hardware programming domains that were previously considered too labor‑intensive. This work suggests that with sufficient prompting and compute resources, AI agents can effectively bridge the gap between high‑level model design and low‑level hardware implementation, potentially accelerating the adoption of custom inference accelerators.

stories.author: archon1410
stories.title: Unforced Navier-Stokes Singularity and the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis
stories.groq_label: AI assisted Lean formalizations claim proofs of finite time blowup for three dimensional Euler and Navier Stokes equations and a Lean only proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis
stories.groq_explain: The post announces three major developments that have been produced with extensive AI assistance and formalized in the Lean proof assistant. First, Levent Alpöge, Tristan Buckmaster, and Matei Coiculescu have created a human‑readable proof that the unforced incompressible Euler equations in three dimensions can develop a finite‑time singularity. The proof is also available as a formal Lean verification. Second, Alpöge and Buckmaster, again using heavy AI support, have generated a proof of finite‑time blowup for the unforced incompressible Navier–Stokes equations in three dimensions. This paper is technically readable and follows a known strategy: constructing an approximate discretely self‑similar solution numerically and then applying rigorous perturbation theory to turn it into an exact solution. Although the overall argument is clear, a fully polished, professionally written version is still pending. Third, Alpöge has produced an enormous Lean‑only proof of the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis. The proof appears to rely on deep recent advances in the Langlands program and arithmetic geometry. Verification of this proof is ongoing in a dedicated Lean Zulip thread, where discussion is now limited to the Lean‑related aspects. The author notes that these results will soon be reported in other outlets and references a Mastodon post by Buckmaster that discusses the first two results. The announcements are significant because they claim breakthroughs on two of the most famous open problems in analysis—the Euler and Navier–Stokes blowup questions—and on a central conjecture in number theory, the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, while also highlighting the emerging role of AI and formal proof assistants in producing and checking complex mathematics.

stories.author: khalidkhair
stories.title: Running two PSP emulators on one Switch 2 and sharing one via GameShare
stories.groq_label: An experimental PPSSPP build runs two isolated emulator instances on a Switch 2 to stream one to another device via GameShare.
stories.groq_explain:
This document details an experimental branch of the PPSSPP emulator, known as ppsspp-nx2, designed for the Nintendo Switch 2. The project experiments with running a second, independent PPSSPP guest emulator on a host Switch 2 console and streaming its display and controls to a second console using the system GameShare feature. Rather than simply mirroring controls or acting as a secondary controller, the setup runs two distinct emulator instances simultaneously inside a single application process on the host console.

Building and installing the experimental software requires specific build scripts and deployment commands with experimental flags enabled. It installs as a separate application alongside the standard single-instance PPSSPP installation, leaving existing host settings, saves, and application files untouched. Launching requires a GameShare-capable native title override, as generic title overrides do not grant the necessary system context for GameShare. To start sharing, the user selects the GameShare option from the host application menu, and the client console joins through its system GameShare screen, allowing both consoles to browse game files stored on the host console SD card.

Underneath the hood, the project links a second PPSSPP core into a relocatable object, renaming all defined core global symbols to ensure strict isolation between the host and guest cores. Both instances possess independent settings, memory stick directories, JIT registries, and Vulkan rendering contexts while sharing the same underlying OS process. The host runs at 1080p resolution at 120 hertz, whereas the guest renders offscreen at 720p targeted at 60 frames per second. Completed guest frames are read back by the CPU and delivered to a separate display layer for streaming. This readback step introduces CPU overhead, meaning zero-copy rendering is not implemented.

Storage, audio, and controller inputs are isolated between the host and guest instances. Guest inputs do not interact with the host emulator, and guest audio is directed to a dedicated per-guest queue, which has been verified to play audio on the client console. Native text-entry applets for the guest are currently disabled due to missing remote routing capabilities. For local PSP ad hoc multiplayer, the application runs a local packet relay and discovery service on loopback ports on the host console. Because both emulator instances physically run on the host Switch 2, multiplayer traffic remains entirely internal without needing external network relays, Wi-Fi IP configuration, or UPnP setup.

This experiment is significant because it explores multi-instance emulation and single-console hosting of remote multiplayer gaming using native Switch 2 hardware features. However, current tests serve as a preliminary technical checkpoint, and compilation and host tests do not yet establish console operation or acceptable performance when actively running two games at the same time.
